evidenceRecords.text: Electro Optic Systems Holdings Limited (EOS) has entered into an agreement with the government of a Middle Eastern Gulf state (a Gulf Co-operation Council member) for the provision of a nationwide, counter-uncrewed aerial system (C-UAS) defence system valued at GBP 370 million.
EOS said on 9 October that this is the largest contract the company has secured.
The company’s NiDAR C-UAS system, acquired as part of the recent MARSS acquisition, is central to the contract.
It is an AI-enabled command and control system (C2), designed specifically for C-UAS defence, covering both airborne and coastal seaborne drone detection.
The contract requires the rapid deployment of a cellular, nationwide C-UAS system with NiDAR C2.
EOS is acting as the prime contractor and systems integrator.

items.originalTitle: Blackbeard Hypersonic Missile Shown Being Fired From Ground Launcher
items.summary: Castelion has released what appears to be the first image of its relatively ‘cheap’ Blackbeard hypersonic missile being fired from a ground launcher, providing a new look at the containerized launch architecture now under development for the U.S. Army. The photograph, posted by Castelion on X, shows a Blackbeard missile leaving a launcher mounted on a high-mobility truck chassis. While the missile itself is by now a familiar sight , the new image offers a first public glimpse of how Castelion intends to package and operate the ground-launched version of Blackbeard, known as Blackbeard GL.

Built to move with the fight. pic.twitter.com/OzWbiChCPQ — Castelion (@Castelion) October 8, 2026 The Army’s previously disclosed plans for the program call for an initial Blackbeard ground-launch demonstration using a modified Multiple Launch Rocket System Family of Munitions , or MFOM, pod, followed by the development of Blackbeard GL prototypes and a dedicated launcher pod.

Blackbeard for HIMARS. pic.twitter.com/uA9XgcGvsI — Castelion (@Castelion) August 3, 2026 The Army’s Fiscal Year 2027 budget documentation indicates that this effort is moving toward increasingly representative hardware.
Among the milestones listed for FY2027 is a live-fire launch of a “production representative” Blackbeard GL and launcher pod.
Castelion has already released extensive imagery of Blackbeard test vehicles, and the company formally unveiled the weapon’s current external configuration earlier this year .

items.summary: As the Golden Age of deep-space exploration begins, NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy are advancing the development of safe, reliable, next-generation nuclear technologies for space. Together, the agencies will supercharge civil space exploration, unlock bold scientific discovery, and solidify American leadership in space nuclear power and propulsion. “We are entering the ‘Nuclear NASA-era,’ which represents a major transformation for space exploration,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

evidenceRecords.text: As the Golden Age of deep-space exploration begins, NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy are advancing the development of safe, reliable, next-generation nuclear technologies for space.
Together, the agencies will supercharge civil space exploration, unlock bold scientific discovery, and solidify American leadership in space nuclear power and propulsion.
“We are entering the ‘Nuclear NASA-era,’ which represents a major transformation for space exploration,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

The work we’re doing today is laying the foundation for the fission-powered spacecraft of tomorrow and opening an entirely new frontier for exploration and discovery.” The new Memorandum of Understanding, “Accelerating American Leadership in Space Nuclear Power and Propulsion,” was signed Thursday between NASA and DOE, and establishes a framework for end-to-end collaboration.
The agreement unites both agencies across the full spectrum of space nuclear development, spanning advanced research and fuel production to rigorous testing, launch integration, and operations.
The signing took place between Isaacman and U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright during the Science: A Golden Age Summit, hosted by the Office of Science and Technology Policy at the Donald J.
“Thanks to President Trump, America’s nuclear renaissance is reaching a new frontier,” said Wright.

“The Energy Department is proud to partner with NASA as we help American space missions reach uncharted territory.” President Trump’s December 2025 Executive Order on Ensuring American Space Superiority directs NASA to develop a launch-ready lunar surface reactor by 2030, a goal toward which NASA, partnering with DOE, is making steady progress.

This pivotal agreement fortifies existing collaborations on fission and radioisotope power systems, propelling NASA’s vision for a sustained human presence on the Moon and accelerating the breakthrough technologies to enable our mission.
When NASA’s Space Reactor‑1 Freedom launches in 2028, nuclear propulsion will advance from laboratory research to operational deep‑space application.
This milestone paves the way for Lunar Reactor‑1, the fission surface power system that will sustain the future Moon Base through darkness and shadow.

items.title: izmo Microsystems and IIT Madras Advance ₹99.94 Crore Silicon Photonics Program
items.originalTitle: izmo Microsystems and IIT Madras Advance ₹99.94 Crore Silicon Photonics Program
items.summary: Insider Brief izmo Microsystems and IIT Madras have entered Phase II of the Centre for Programmable Photonic Integrated Circuits and Systems (CPPICS), a five-year silicon photonics program with a total outlay of ₹99.94 crore. The SPECTRA program will target silicon photonics applications in data-center transceivers, microwave photonics, quantum technologies and photonic computing for AI. izmo Microsystems will contribute packaging, testing and integration expertise, including work on co-packaged optics and a 1.6 Tbps silicon photonics transceiver engine.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief izmo Microsystems and IIT Madras have entered Phase II of the Centre for Programmable Photonic Integrated Circuits and Systems (CPPICS), a five-year silicon photonics program with a total outlay of ₹99.94 crore.

The SPECTRA program will target silicon photonics applications in data-center transceivers, microwave photonics, quantum technologies and photonic computing for AI. izmo Microsystems will contribute packaging, testing and integration expertise, including work on co-packaged optics and a 1.6 Tbps silicon photonics transceiver engine.
PRESS RELEASE — izmo Limited (NSE: IZMO) (BSE: 532341) today announced that its semiconductor subsidiary, izmo Microsystems Pvt.

Ltd., has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding with the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) for Phase II of the Centre for Programmable Photonic Integrated Circuits and Systems (CPPICS).

The Phase II program, titled Silicon Photonics Enabled Cutting-edge Technology Research and Applications (SPECTRA) , has been sanctioned by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, with a total project outlay of ₹99.94 crore.
The five-year program includes a MeitY contribution of ₹97.54 crore and a ₹2.40 crore cash and in-kind commitment from izmo Microsystems.

CPPICS Phase II is designed to advance silicon photonics technologies from research towards commercially deployable products, covering photonic integrated circuit design, fabrication, characterization, advanced packaging, testing and system integration.
Silicon Photonics for the AI infrastructure era The program comes at a time when optical connectivity is becoming critical infrastructure for AI and high-performance computing.

The program also proposes development of a silicon photonics Process Design Kit incorporating more than 100 IP blocks for 200 mm wafer platforms, supporting the design and manufacture of increasingly complex photonic integrated circuits. izmo Microsystems to Drive Packaging and Industrialization A key challenge in silicon photonics is converting a fabricated photonic chip into a reliable and manufacturable optical system.
CPPICS Phase II brings together IIT Madras’ silicon photonics research capabilities with izmo Microsystems’ advanced packaging and manufacturing expertise.

items.summary: Standing on the deck of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln , Secretary Pete Hegseth looked up at the flattop’s superstructure and got a good indication of many of the targets the Lincoln Carrier Strike Group (CSG) destroyed during its six-month fight with Iran . evidenceRecords.text: Standing on the deck of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln , Secretary Pete Hegseth looked up at the flattop’s superstructure and got a good indication of many of the targets the Lincoln Carrier Strike Group (CSG) destroyed during its six-month fight with Iran .
In a photograph shared by the Pentagon’s image distribution site, Hegseth is seen examining a wall of so-called kill marks stenciled onto the superstructure.
By our count from the image and a video taken during Hegseth’s visit, both of which you can see below, there are 103 one-way attack (OWA) drone kill marks and 34 ship kill marks.
It is unclear whether there are other kill marks we can’t see.
Though they resemble Shahed-136s, which are the most notorious of Iranian OWA drones, these silhouettes would represent all types shot down, and Iran has many.

Defense Secretary @PeteHegseth awards Presidential Unit Citation to USS Abraham Lincoln pic.twitter.com/DbS5YYu9oB — CSPAN (@cspan) October 7, 2026 It is unclear at the moment why there are at least 26 more drone kill marks stenciled onto the Lincoln than the number of drones shot down listed in the unit citation and why there are 30 fewer ship kill marks than the tally noted in the citation.

items.title: Technology Used by Optical Atomic Clocks May Jump From Lab to Consumer
items.originalTitle: Technology Used by Optical Atomic Clocks May Jump From Lab to Consumer
items.summary: Insider Brief University of Auckland and U.S. researchers demonstrated a chip-based optical frequency comb that could support smaller precision measurement systems, including portable atomic clocks. The researchers demonstrated precise optical frequency generation, low-noise millimetre-wave signals and optical clock readout, with potential applications in navigation, telecommunications and sensing. So far, the laser tools called optical frequency combs have been trapped in the lab because of their size and expense.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief University of Auckland and U.S. researchers demonstrated a chip-based optical frequency comb that could support smaller precision measurement systems, including portable atomic clocks.

The researchers demonstrated precise optical frequency generation, low-noise millimetre-wave signals and optical clock readout, with potential applications in navigation, telecommunications and sensing.
So far, the laser tools called optical frequency combs have been trapped in the lab because of their size and expense.
Optical frequency combs are the standard tools for measuring the frequency – or colours – of light.

But research by University of Auckland and US scientists, reported in the prestigious journal Nature, suggests a new path for shrinking the technology to chip size for future navigation systems, communications networks, precision sensors and portable atomic clocks.

The breakthrough is a culmination of work that started in 2021, when Professor Miro Erkintalo, who is the head of the Department of Physics at the University and a researcher at the Dodd-Walls Centre for Photonic and Quantum Technologies, began exploring a potential new way to generate chip-scale frequency combs.
With the help of his students, he predicted that two laser beams launched into a chip-scale ring could generate a new type of frequency comb.

The prediction became reality in 2024, when the Auckland researchers teamed up with Grégory Moille and Kartik Srinivasan from the University of Maryland and the US National Institute of Science and Technology to successfully demonstrate the idea in the lab.
While the 2024 demonstration was a groundbreaking physics proof-of-concept, breakthrough applications were still unrealized.
Optical frequency combs have enabled the creation of the most precise clocks in the world – optical atomic clocks – and the many other applications have included experiments in basic physics.
Portable optical atomic clocks could help map underground variations in mineral deposits and enable navigation systems that don’t rely on GPS satellite signals.

Reducing the size, weight, power, and cost of optical frequency combs can lead to mass production and move the technology from lab to consumer, Erkintalo and his collaborators write in the Nature paper.

"Secretary Hegseth made it clear: We are done with the bureaucratic inertia holding back modernization,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said in a news release . evidenceRecords.text: The service announced the creation of Futures and Autonomous Systems Command on Friday, a day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of a new combatant command for autonomous warfare in a speech to troops.
"Secretary Hegseth made it clear: We are done with the bureaucratic inertia holding back modernization,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said in a news release .

FASCOM will stand up in the wake of last year’s decision to consolidate Army Futures Command and Training and Doctrine Command , part of a multi-year effort by the service to reduce its general officer ranks .
The difference is that FASCOM will be led by an acquisition executive, where Futures Command had four-star generals with infantry backgrounds at the helm during its short tenure.

Though the command endeavoured to fix the Army’s broken requirements process, ultimately the final decisions and acquisitions were made at the Pentagon, creating a disconnect that FASCOM won’t have to deal with.
Except this time, rather than a standalone four-star command with no joint equivalent, FASCOM could nest under the new Autonomous Warfare Command as a service component.
\"Secretary Hegseth made it clear: We are done with the bureaucratic inertia holding back modernization,\u201d acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said in a news release.\u00a0

FASCOM will stand up in the wake of last year\u2019s decision to consolidate Army Futures Command and Training and Doctrine Command, part of a multi-year effort by the service to reduce its general officer ranks.
Hegseth has since taken the idea military-wide.

Though the command endeavoured to fix the Army\u2019s broken requirements process, ultimately the final decisions and acquisitions were made at the Pentagon, creating a disconnect that FASCOM won\u2019t have to deal with.
\u201cSo maybe this is kind of Futures Command 2.0, right?\u201d John G.
Ferrari, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and retired two-star general, told Defense One.

\u201cI think their theory of the case is that you have too many disparate organizations within the Pentagon working this, and that they're working in some cases counter to each other,\u201d Ferrari said, referring to the Defense Innovation Unit, various service PAEs and the recently created Defense Autonomous Warfare Group.

A combatant command \u201cgives a single military leader the authority, the responsibility, and the resources to drive this,\u201d he said. \u201cSo I think it's an admission that the current organizational structure isn't going to deliver in a timely manner.\u201d

evidenceRecords.text: Shield AI announced that the U.S. Navy has executed a $150 million modification to its existing Other Transaction (OT) agreement with the company to advance X-BAT, an AI-piloted, vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) fighter aircraft.

Shield AI press release The Navy executed the $150 million modification with funding from the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment through its Defense Exportability Features program.
Shield AI will invest $150 million of its own capital in X-BAT alongside the government funding.

In August, the Department of the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive (Aviation) Rapid Capability Cell [PAE(A) RCC], in partnership with the Defense Innovation Unit (DIU), announced a separate $50 million funding action for X-BAT under the Runway Independent Maritime Expeditionary Strike (RIMES) effort.
This action was a separate prior modification to the existing OT agreement referenced here.
Shield AI independently committed $50 million of private capital alongside that effort.
The two actions, together with Shield AI’s investments, bring announced public and private commitments to X-BAT to $400 million.
Across the broader X-BAT program, a team of 500 engineers at Shield AI and key suppliers, including GE Aerospace, is building flight-test aircraft.
Shield AI’s Hivemind software serves as X-BAT’s AI pilot, enabling operations in GPS-denied and communications-constrained conditions.
“We are testing early and often while working on the aircraft, mission systems, ship suitability and production in parallel,” said Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft at Shield AI.

“That approach helps us identify and resolve issues earlier, reduce development risk and move more quickly toward flight testing.” X-BAT is scheduled to begin flight testing later this year and is a component of DIU’s RIMES Project, a multifaceted effort across industry intended to provide Combatant Commanders with long range strike assets capable of taking off and landing vertically from ships, islands and austere sites, extending strategic reach of surface and expeditionary assets without dependence on fixed runways.
“X-BAT is being built to enhance the lethality, survivability and combat power of U.S. Naval Aviation,” said J.J.

items.summary: Exail introduced its Neptis uncrewed maritime surveillance system during the Euronaval press tour. Bringing together Oryx-family uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), mission-specific sensors and command-and-control software, the system can be configured for maritime surveillance, anti-submarine warfare and the protection of critical underwater infrastructure. Exail describes Neptis as a “system of systems” designed to support persistent operations in maritime areas where access is restricted or the threat level is high.

evidenceRecords.text: Exail introduced its Neptis uncrewed maritime surveillance system during the Euronaval press tour.

Bringing together Oryx-family uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), mission-specific sensors and command-and-control software, the system can be configured for maritime surveillance, anti-submarine warfare and the protection of critical underwater infrastructure.
Exail describes Neptis as a “system of systems” designed to support persistent operations in maritime areas where access is restricted or the threat level is high.
Oryx vessels carry sensors into the area of operations, while Neptis command-and-control software manages platform supervision and communications and presents collected information to operators.

Software interface of the Neptis system (Exail picture) The demonstrated capabilities were limited to platform supervision, tactical track visualisation, operator-led preliminary assessment and intelligence support.
Neptis’ intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions include monitoring sea lines of communication, strategic passages, ports and exclusive economic zone boundaries.

items.title: Pentagon barred Qatar base access to hide Iran war damage, US senator claims
items.originalTitle: Pentagon barred Qatar base access to hide Iran war damage, US senator claims
items.summary: A U.S. senator was recently denied access to the largest military installation in the Middle East, calling it a “cover-up” over the damage suffered during the Iran war . Chris Murphy, D-Conn., visited the Middle East this week on a Congressional Delegation trip, speaking with Gulf region leaders and visiting American facilities to assess damage done by the Iran war. Murphy was denied access to Al Udeid Air Base , Qatar, which had suffered damage from drone strikes during the conflict.

evidenceRecords.text: A U.S. senator was recently denied access to the largest military installation in the Middle East, calling it a “cover-up” over the damage suffered during the Iran war .
Chris Murphy, D-Conn., visited the Middle East this week on a Congressional Delegation trip, speaking with Gulf region leaders and visiting American facilities to assess damage done by the Iran war.
Murphy was denied access to Al Udeid Air Base , Qatar, which had suffered damage from drone strikes during the conflict.

“They are using every tool they can, including withholding information about damages, slow walking the pace of reports about casualties and denying us access to see the damage as part of a campaign of cover-up, so as to mask the true cost of the war,” Murphy told reporters on Thursday.

The “unprecedented” base denial prepared Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and Defense Appropriations Committee, in the coming days to draft language that would explicitly require the Department of Defense to grant members of Congress access to military bases overseas under all circumstances if needed.
Prior to his trip, Murphy requested access to the base through a letter and direct appeal to U.S. Central Command leadership.
But he was denied access even as the Department of State supported his trip to the region, with the Defense Department saying it was due to previously imposed travel restrictions.

“Senator Murphy’s office was informed before his trip to the Middle East that he would not receive Department of War support to access Al Udeid Air Base, consistent with the Secretary of War’s directive on travel restrictions in the region ordered on March 3, 2026,” a senior Defense Department official told Military Times on Thursday.
“That decision was communicated in advance by the Office of the Secretary of War for Legislative Affairs,” the official continued.

“The Department applies the Secretary’s guidance evenly.” In early March, the State and Defense departments issued travel guidance, calling on Americans to depart areas in the region and updating its travel advisory to recommend against visiting certain countries, including Qatar.

evidenceRecords.text: The $1.1 billion program is the Pentagon’s effort to rapidly expand the domestic drone industry by having companies submit small unmanned aircraft systems, or sUASs, for competition and then building stockpiles of the systems that perform best for military use.
Erin Cherry, the program’s test lead, told Military Times in an email that DIU is looking to recruit about 100 pilots for the program’s next phase, known as Gauntlet III.
But the larger goal is to create a standing registry of drone operators across the military services.

“We want to hear from any warfighter with FPV experience.” She explained that service members selected to participate will get “stick time” with some of the newest drones, including systems that are not yet in military service, and some will receive specialized training on one-way attack drones .
“Most importantly, Gauntlet results strongly inform which systems move forward, and these pilots are the ones flying,” Cherry said.
“There’s no cap on the registry,” Cherry said. “We want to hear from any warfighter with FPV experience.”

She explained that service members selected to participate will get “stick time” with some of the newest drones, including systems that are not yet in military service, and some will receive specialized training on one-way attack drones.
But Cherry said DIU is looking for more than just experienced FPV pilots.
That variety is important because the drones will ultimately be used by more than just the military’s most experienced operators.

“A drone that only performs well in an expert’s hands isn’t ready for the force,” Cherry said, adding that “whether someone has been flying FPV for five years or five months, we want to hear from them.”
For service members interested in participating, DIU is asking them to complete a Pilot Interest Form.
Officials will only respond to applicants using a valid .mil email address, and all pilot participation will be coordinated through the individual military services.
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times.

items.title: France to start training Ukrainian pilots on Rafale warplanes in November, minister says
items.originalTitle: France to start training Ukrainian pilots on Rafale warplanes in November, minister says
items.summary: PARIS — France will begin training Ukrainian pilots on the Rafale fighter jet next month, Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said in a parliamentary hearing on Thursday. “We are continuing our discussions regarding the combat aviation component, particularly regarding the Rafale,” Vautrin told French lawmakers in response to questions about aid to Ukraine during a 2027 defense-budget hearing here.

evidenceRecords.text: PARIS — France will begin training Ukrainian pilots on the Rafale fighter jet next month, Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said in a parliamentary hearing on Thursday.

“We are continuing our discussions regarding the combat aviation component, particularly regarding the Rafale,” Vautrin told French lawmakers in response to questions about aid to Ukraine during a 2027 defense-budget hearing here.

“From November, we will begin the first training of Ukrainian pilots on Rafale.” Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on Rafale aircraft in France, a major step forward for Ukraine’s combat aviation, the country’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Telegram post on Monday, citing a conversation with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron.
Ukraine in July agreed on a roadmap with France that included a plan to buy 16 Rafale fighter jets together with the accompanying weapon systems.

The country has previously received F-16 jets from several European countries, Mirage 2000 fighters from France, and in May agreed to buy 20 new Gripen jets , with Sweden donating 16 units of an older model.
The first Rafale jets are expected to fly in Ukrainian skies in 2028 or 2029, Macron said in July.
Both countries are continuing to work on localizing production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine, Zelenskyy said on Monday.
Vautrin said in her hearing that a licensing process is currently underway for missiles.
“We are fully aware that by supporting Ukraine, we are defending Europe,” Vautrin said.
As part of the July agreement, Ukraine would also acquire an initial batch of SAMP/T NG air-defense batteries with missiles, Macron said at the time.

PRESS RELEASE — Chattanooga Quantum Collaborative announces seventeen professionals from sixteen Tennessee employers completed the Quantum Ready Pre-Apprenticeship, a 12-week program created by the Chattanooga Quantum Collaborative (CQC) to help companies understand emerging quantum technologies.

The program was designed for professionals already working in technology-adjacent roles, with two goals: upskilling the existing workforce and building quantum proficiency inside the organizations where they work.
“Quantum won’t replace every system overnight, but exploring where it complements classical technology can provide businesses an early, distinct competitive edge,” said Charlie Brock, CEO of CQC.

“This program puts early advocates directly into the companies best positioned to benefit, equipping them to test real-world quantum applications and address complex business challenges classical computing alone can’t resolve.” “Research opens the door to new possibilities, and industry adoption carries that work into economic impact,” said Mina Sartipi, Interim Vice Chancellor for Research at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga .

Every trip or vehicle you add multiplies the number of possible schedules, so I identified where quantum optimization could come in once current methods reach their limits.” The Quantum Ready Pre-Apprenticeship was delivered through the BuildWithin platform and supported by a National Science Foundation planning grant awarded to the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga , with CQC serving as a subawardee focused on workforce and industry engagement.

PRESS RELEASE — Arqit Quantum Inc. (Nasdaq: ARQQ) (“Arqit”), a global leader in quantum-safe encryption, announces select preliminary financial results for the second half and full fiscal year 2026.
Based on preliminary unaudited results, management expects revenue for the second half period ended 30 September 2026 of approximately $355,000 to $380,000.
For the full fiscal year ended 30 September 2026, revenue is expected to be $975,000 to $1,000,000.
Cash and cash equivalents were approximately $51 million as of 30 September 2026.
Revenue for the second half period ended 30 September 2026 was down as compared to revenue of $463,000 for the same period in fiscal year 2025.
Revenue for the full fiscal ended 30 September 2026 compares favourably to revenue of $530,000 for fiscal year 2025.

Growth in revenue for fiscal year 2026 versus fiscal year 2025 resulted from but was not limited to: Revenue recognition associated with delivery under contracts signed prior to the commencement of the period; and Revenue recognition associated with 7 new contracts signed in the period.
Revenue for the second half of fiscal year 2026 was adversely affected by cessation of revenue recognition under a material contract with a customer in the Middle East.
The preliminary financial results discussed in this press release are based on management’s preliminary unaudited analysis of financial results for the second half and full fiscal year 2026.

items.title: Future cost, use of Marine Corps ACVs scrutinized in congressional report
items.originalTitle: Future cost, use of Marine Corps ACVs scrutinized in congressional report
items.summary: With today’s armored vehicles vulnerable to drones, congressional researchers are raising questions about the U.S. Marine Corps’ new Amphibious Combat Vehicle . In particular, a Congressional Research Service report , released Tuesday, pointed to the war in Ukraine, where armored vehicles have largely been driven from the battlefield by unmanned aerial vehicles and guided munitions.

evidenceRecords.text: With today’s armored vehicles vulnerable to drones, congressional researchers are raising questions about the U.S. Marine Corps’ new Amphibious Combat Vehicle .

In particular, a Congressional Research Service report , released Tuesday, pointed to the war in Ukraine, where armored vehicles have largely been driven from the battlefield by unmanned aerial vehicles and guided munitions.

“As ACVs are intended to provide organic, direct fire support to dismounted Marines in the attack, how vulnerable to these threat systems are ACVs during amphibious operations and when operating ashore to support combat operations?” the research service asked in its report.

“Are the Marines considering additional ACV survivability modifications based on lessons learned in Ukraine?” In fact, the Marine Corps did award a contract last month to Anduril for a counter-UAS system to protect the ACV from small drones.

“The system is currently in use by the Special Operations Command due to the system’s low weight, proven performance in engaging multiple UASs, and simultaneous execution of the full kill-chain while static or on the move,” noted the Marine contract award.
The Congressional Research Service also questioned whether a possible plan to expand the Marine Corps would, in turn, require more ACVs, which cost about $6 million each, depending on the variant.
If the plan is implemented, “would additional ACVs be required to accommodate growth in Marine infantry units?” CRS asked.
The ACV comes in multiple variants, including the ACV-P troop carrier, ACV-C command vehicle, ACV-30 fire support model armed with a 30mm cannon, and the ACV-R armored recovery vehicle.
But the current plan is for 608 vehicles, comprising 389 ACV-P, 33 ACV-C, 152 ACV-30 and 34 ACV-R, Marine Corps officials told CRS.
BAE was just awarded a $230 million contract modification for 32 ACV-Rs, which will be the final ACV variant.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Elements , developers of software shortening the path to fault-tolerant quantum computing, today announced that its Constellation platform has been named a winner of TMCnet’z inaugural 2026 Quantum Computing Product of the Year Awards.
Constellation gives quantum teams a hardware-aware development environment, running on classical computer architecture, to design, test and analyze quantum systems before committing to hardware runs.
It allows quantum hardware teams to understand noise, test error-correction strategies, and evaluate decoder performance.

“Constellation is bridging the gap between experimental hardware to fault-tolerant system design by giving development teams a faster, safer, and more repeatable way to validate ideas, improve designs, and prepare workflows for real-world deployment,” said Izhar Medalsy, co-founder and CEO of Quantum Elements .

“We are honored by this recognition of the important role we are playing in advancing towards fault-tolerant quantum computers.” “On behalf of TMCnet and our editors, I’m pleased to recognize Quantum Elements as a winner of the inaugural 2026 Quantum Computing Product of the Year Awards,” said Rich Tehrani, TMCnet’s CEO and Group Editor-in-Chief.

“Constellation represents the kind of innovation that is helping move quantum computing forward—from extraordinary science toward technologies that organizations can access, develop and ultimately put to work.

We congratulate Quantum Elements on this achievement and are proud to recognize it as part of the first class of Quantum Computing Product of the Year Award winners.” The Quantum Computing Product of the Year Awards recognize outstanding products and solutions advancing the quantum computing ecosystem and helping move quantum applications and broader commercial adoption.
Winners of the 2026 Quantum Computing Product of the Year Awards are published on TMCnet.

evidenceRecords.text: Credit: NASA/Keegan Barber After more than seven months aboard the International Space Station, NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission safely splashed down Thursday in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles.
EDT, Thursday, Oct. 15, at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

“Jessica, Jack, Sophie, and Andrey spent 237 days living and working in orbit, traveled more than 100 million miles, advanced important science, and returned safely home because of the extraordinary expertise and competence of thousands across NASA, SpaceX, and our international partners,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

“Building the capability, experience, and confidence to do this repeatedly is exactly what will allow us to go farther, and I am grateful to Crew-12 and their families for their service to humanity’s greatest adventure.” NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway , ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev returned to Earth at 8:34 a.m.
Teams aboard SpaceX recovery vessels retrieved the spacecraft and its crew shortly after.
Following standard postflight medical screenings, the crew will fly to shore before returning to NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

“NASA’s activities supporting the International Space Station — transporting crew, conducting impactful research, and maintaining critical national assets — enable the science, engineering, and risk‑reduction needed for future missions across the solar system,” said Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program at the agency’s Johnson Space Center.
Crew-12 lifted off at 5:15 a.m.
Crew‑12 logged hundreds of hours of scientific research to support human exploration beyond low Earth orbit and advance benefits for people on Earth.

items.title: What does the UK public really think about BVLOS operations?
items.originalTitle: What does the UK public really think about BVLOS operations?
items.summary: Noise has long-been a complaint when it comes to public acceptance of drone operations. FFSI also noted that respondents did not evaluate drone use cases in isolation. “When asked to reason about medical, police and commercial delivery drone use together, as parts of a single emerging system, support does not simply accumulate from the most popular use cases outward,” FFSI explained.

evidenceRecords.text: Noise has long-been a complaint when it comes to public acceptance of drone operations.
FFSI also noted that respondents did not evaluate drone use cases in isolation.

“When asked to reason about medical, police and commercial delivery drone use together, as parts of a single emerging system, support does not simply accumulate from the most popular use cases outward,” FFSI explained.

“Instead, a meaningful proportion of the public who recognise clear benefits in specific applications nonetheless judge that the overall balance of benefits and drawbacks is unfavourable once the full system is considered, and association with less trusted or less clearly necessary applications – such as some commercial delivery uses that were viewed as more frivolous – can actively undermine support for more beneficial ones, including medical and emergency use.” This finding directly challenges assumptions underpinning the ‘drones for good’ argument and indicates that public trust must be
FFSI found that the UK public is “broadly supportive, engaged and discerning, rather than simply optimistic or resistant”.

There is public support for drone operations and this can be strong but also conditional on transparency, proportionality, genuine accountability, cross-sector coordination and meaningful involvement in how these systems are designed and deployed.

To address the survey’s findings, FFSI has set out five recommendations: Establish transparent and accountable oversight structures, closing current gaps between regulators and creating genuine mechanisms for citizen input and establishing new oversight mechanisms where existing bodies were not designed to cover the range of concerns, issues or risks that emerging drone systems and services present.
Deliver early and meaningful public engagement that feeds into real decisions at both local and national levels.
Invest in continued, independent research to track attitudes and inform policy as BVLOS operations scale up.
FFSI said that the window to act on these recommendations is open now, while operations are scaling, but will narrow as BVLOS drone use becomes routine.

The attack late on Thursday was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom and allied forces in neighbouring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Three Saudi citizens have been killed and several other people were wounded in attacks targeting Riyadh ⁠airport for which Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility, Saudi officials have said.
The first attack on Thursday afternoon targeted airport facilities, while the second struck aircraft, the Saudi statement said.
It did not identify those responsible, though the Houthis claimed to have targeted the airport with a ballistic missile.
Among the dead was Capt Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, the Saudia Group said in a statement.
It appeared to be the first confirmed attack on the Saudi national carrier since the new offensive began.
A separate Saudia Group statement said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers onboard.
The aviation statement said the injuries to citizens and people of other nationalities “ranged from minor to serious”.
The Saudia Group statement said operational activities at the airport returned to normal at 6pm on Thursday, hours after the attack.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in ​Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to ‌take back territory from the Houthis.
The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz.

items.title: Cargo drones deliver maintenance kits to North Sea wind turbines
items.originalTitle: Cargo drones deliver maintenance kits to North Sea wind turbines
items.summary: Ørsted and Skyports Drone Services have completed a four-week cargo drone trial at the Hornsea 2 offshore wind farm in the North Sea, delivering maintenance kits weighing up to 65kg directly to active wind turbines. The trial was Ørsted’s most complex offshore cargo drone operation to date and included the company’s first beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) cargo delivery within the wind farm. The drone flew around 4km between a specialist service vessel and individual turbines, with flights planned, coordinated and monitored from the vessel.

The maintenance kits contained tools, spare parts and materials for specific turbine maintenance tasks.
Following delivery, the drone collected the kits and returned them to the service vessel.
The trial also introduced an automatic hook system attached to the drone’s winch, removing the need for an operator to manually connect the cargo bag.

items.summary: First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe. Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again. Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date. Their finding has implications for what kind of energetic event creates these bursts. “What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them.

Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again.
Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date.
“What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don’t know what generates them.
The MeerTRAP team used the MeerKAT telescope to detect the burst on March 4, 2024, leading to its designation as FRB 20240304B.
The radio data from this burst suggested that it was extremely distant, possibly the most distant one seen to date.
To confirm that distance, though, astronomers would need to study its host galaxy.
Although they knew the location of the FRB very precisely, the world’s largest ground-based telescopes could not see any galaxy at that spot in the sky.
As a result, the team turned to the Webb telescope.
The team discovered that the host galaxy of FRB 20240304B was not typical of other galaxies with FRBs.
First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe.
Their finding has implications for what kind of energetic event creates these bursts.
“What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them.

We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof,” said Manisha Caleb of the University of Sydney, lead author on the study published Thursday in the journal Science.

Webb’s NIRCam (Near-Infrared Camera) instrument detected a galaxy in the right location, and its NIRSpec (Near-Infrared Spectrograph) instrument provided a precise measurement of the galaxy’s redshift: 2.148, corresponding to a time just 3 billion years after the big bang.
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope’s NIRCam (Near-Infrared Camera) was able to detect the host galaxy of the fast radio burst called FRB 20240304B, whose location is shown by the white cross.
Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope were able to study the host galaxy of the most distant known fast radio burst (FRB).

items.title: Quobly and SiPearl Partner to Explore European CPU-QPU Integration For Sovereign Quantum Computing
items.originalTitle: Quobly and SiPearl Partner to Explore European CPU-QPU Integration For Sovereign Quantum Computing
items.summary: Insider Brief Quobly and SiPearl signed a non-exclusive agreement to explore combining silicon spin quantum processors with European CPUs to support a sovereign European quantum computing system. The initial phase will assess integrating SiPearl’s Rhea1 CPU and Seine reference server with a Quobly quantum processor system for its Alloy product line, followed by exploration of hybrid computing workloads and future architectures.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Quobly and SiPearl signed a non-exclusive agreement to explore combining silicon spin quantum processors with European CPUs to support a sovereign European quantum computing system.

The initial phase will assess integrating SiPearl’s Rhea1 CPU and Seine reference server with a Quobly quantum processor system for its Alloy product line, followed by exploration of hybrid computing workloads and future architectures.

PRESS RELEASE — Quobly , a French quantum computing company developing industrially scalable quantum computers based on silicon spin qubits, and SiPearl, the designer of European high-performance energy-efficient CPUs for sovereign supercomputing, AI and data centre, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to combine their respective technologies and expertise towards a sovereign quantum computing solution, bringing together SiPearl’s CPU technology and Quobly ’s quantum processors.

Integrating European CPU and quantum technologies This non-exclusive collaboration will initially focus on integrating SiPearl’s first-generation Rhea1 CPU and its associated Seine reference server with a Quobly QPU system, as part of the development of Quobly’s Alloy product line.

Supporting a European sovereign computing ecosystem The collaboration brings together two core building blocks for European computing, combining SiPearl’s CPU technology with Quobly ’s quantum processors, and marks a first step towards bridging Europe’s HPC and quantum computing ecosystems.
SiPearl and Quobly also intend to coordinate their efforts to respond to European calls for tenders, including potential joint opportunities under the Chips Joint Undertaking (Chips JU) on Quantum.

By exploring the integration of SiPearl’s CPU technology with our quantum computers, we are looking at how HPC and quantum computing can work together efficiently, from the system level to future architectures.

“We have had close ties with Quobly for a long time, thanks in particular to SiPearl’s R&D centre in Grenoble, but above all because we share the same vision regarding the need to build a European hardware ecosystem for sovereign computing.

This first partnership with a quantum expert marks another significant milestone in the development of this ecosystem which will offer complementary sovereign hardware solutions in the fields of HPC, AI and quantum computing for Europe’s strategic applications”, concluded Philippe Notton, CEO and Founder of SiPearl.

items.title: FAA puts $12 million behind 19 drone research projects
items.originalTitle: FAA puts $12 million behind 19 drone research projects
items.summary: The FAA is putting more money into the technologies it believes could help drones safely become a bigger part of the US airspace. The agency has announced $12 million in awards for 19 companies and organizations working on drone research and testing projects. The funding comes through the FAA’s Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) Program, which supports commercial entities working with FAA-designated UAS Test Sites.

The FAA is putting more money into the technologies it believes could help drones safely become a bigger part of the US airspace.
The funding comes through the FAA’s Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Broad Agency Announcement (BAA) Program, which supports commercial entities working with FAA-designated UAS Test Sites.

The goal is fairly straightforward: test the technology in real-world conditions, collect better data, and figure out what still needs to be solved before more drones can routinely share the National Airspace System with airplanes and other aircraft.

“The UAS Broad Agency Announcement Program gives us another way to directly work with industry and our test site partners on technologies that are critical to safe drone integration,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford explains.
The research, he adds, will help the agency identify operational challenges and inform how drones can be safely integrated into the national airspace.
The projects cover a surprisingly broad range of problems.

General Atomics and OneRadio are working on technologies designed to help drones detect and avoid other aircraft, while Skydweller is developing onboard systems for large drones to perform similar functions.
NAVMAR is also working on systems intended to support the safe operation of larger drones.
Long-distance drone operations are another major theme.
Censys Technologies will test satellite communications for long-range flights, while Lighthouse Avionics is working on surveillance technology for extended drone routes.
Devorto Corporation, meanwhile, is tackling the practical side of long-range cargo drone services.

items.title: German Budget Committee approves procurement of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU-class frigates
items.originalTitle: German Budget Committee approves procurement of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU-class frigates
items.summary: On October 8, 2026, the Budget Committee of the German Bundestag approved the procurement of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU frigates from TKMS at its meeting. This brings the total number of identical MEKO frigates procured to eight, as stated in a press release from the Federal Ministry of Defense. According to well-informed sources, approximately five billion euros have been allocated for this purpose. The committee had already given the green light for the procurement of the first four frigates of this type on July 8th. The industry has committed to starting delivery of the ships in 2029.

evidenceRecords.text: On October 8, 2026, the Budget Committee of the German Bundestag approved the procurement of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU frigates from TKMS at its meeting.
By Hartpunkt This brings the total number of identical MEKO frigates procured to eight, as stated in a press release from the Federal Ministry of Defense.
The committee had already given the green light for the procurement of the first four frigates of this type on July 8th.
The frigates are to be procured primarily for anti-submarine warfare.
The German Federal Ministry of Defence (BMVg) writes that NATO has been promised a wide range of capability contributions within the framework of capability and defense planning.

In addition to other capabilities, the navy will make a significant contribution to defense and deterrence in the North and Baltic Seas, as well as in the Atlantic and the High North, through its sea-based anti-submarine warfare capabilities.
The F-126 frigate was originally intended for sea-based anti-submarine warfare.

The German Navy has therefore examined market-available alternatives and confirmed that the MEKO A-200 DEU-class frigates are suitable for anti-submarine warfare and fulfilling Germany’s NATO obligations.
Furthermore, the procurement of eight frigates of a uniform ship type offers the German Navy significant advantages in terms of operation, maintenance, and training.
This brings the total number of identical MEKO frigates procured to eight, as stated in a press release from the Federal Ministry of Defense.
According to well-informed sources, approximately five billion euros have been allocated for this purpose.
The industry has committed to starting delivery of the ships in 2029.

Following significant performance issues, the federal government, after a comprehensive overall assessment, ultimately withdrew from the contract with the general contractor, Damen Werft, the ministry writes.

items.summary: ANKARA — Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militants under a joint defense pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations. evidenceRecords.text: ANKARA — Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militants under a joint defense pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The three countries have since held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.

On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defense commitments and ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan stressed that the pact was defensive rather than offensive, saying military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defense, electronic warfare and technical support.
“Yemen’s legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them,” Fidan said.
When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defense.
Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory,” he said.
Fidan said military delegations would determine Saudi Arabia’s operational defense needs and what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could make.
On Wednesday, two officials told Reuters that Turkey was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help its fight with Houthi militants.
Turkish officials have said any support provided at this stage would largely be in a bilateral capacity, as Turkey’s parliament has not officially ratified the joint defense pact.

Fidan said on Thursday that work was largely completed for the agreement to be submitted for parliament’s approval and that they aimed to send it “as soon as possible.” Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest army and a robust defense industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh’s technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

Since then, OpenAI hasn't caught a break, lurching from one incident to the next.

The firing of three safety researchers tied to the incident has made things worse.

The firings were abrupt and public, and they've spread fear across the team. "If conduct that was considered normal last month now constitutes grounds for sudden dismissal, everyone at OpenAI is left guessing where the line is," the letter reads.
Tomek Korbak, one of the three, described his firing on X.
He was called into a meeting with the head of the safety department, where he was told OpenAI no longer trusted him.
A security officer took his badge and walked him out of the building.
He then learned that his colleagues Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni had also been fired.

evidenceRecords.text: A U.S. Army flight simulator at a barracks in Germany stands as a center of critical training for NATO’s aviation community.

The U.S. Army Garrison Ansbach’s Stock Barracks in Illesheim houses the Illesheim Flight Simulator Complex, or IFSC, providing one-of-a-kind training opportunities ahead of the German Armed Forces preparing to field CH‑47F Block II Chinook helicopters next fall, according to an Army release .

The IFSC, which is operated by U.S. Army Europe and Africa, provides the necessary training needed to prepare German forces to receive 60 of the heavy-lift, tandem-rotor helicopters, the release says.
Two German Air Force pilots who will be part of the first cohort to fly the new aircraft once they arrive in fall 2027 recently trained at the IFSC.
“In the simulator you can train all the scenarios you do not want to experience while flying a real aircraft,” said Lt.
L, a visiting pilot whose name was withheld, as is standard in the German Air Force, or Bundeswehr Luftwaffe.

“Emergency procedures, challenging landings and extreme weather operations can all be practiced safely.” “Everything you can do in a real flight, you can also do in a simulator,” the other visiting pilot, Maj.
The fleet will be stationed at two Bundeswehr installations and is meant to boost Germany’s heavy-lift and transport abilities, per the statement.
The two German pilots also trained in the U.S. Army Aviation Center of Excellence at Fort Rucker, Alabama.
Fort Rucker is the Army’s largest helicopter training institution and trains more than 1,300 U.S. soldiers every year.

The Army did not say how many German aviators are expected to train at Fort Rucker each year, but the release noted that the German Air Force plans to staff more than 200 trained pilots to operate its future fleet.

Since the IFSC simulator software is tailored to U.S. Army aircraft configurations and not the Bundeswehr’s, the German pilots will need additional learning to transition to their Air Force’s aircraft.

The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi.

evidenceRecords.text: WASHINGTON – Raytheon has secured another multi-year munition deal, this time for up to $6.3 billion for Standard Missile-3 Block IB production, the Pentagon announced today.
The base value of the five-year contract is $4.4 billion, but options include an additional nearly $2 billion for more of the air defense munitions over another two years.
The announcement did not say how many of the missiles were under order.

“This contract provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required to dominate the battle space — air, sea or land,” Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey said in a DoD release.
The Pentagon has listed the SB-3 IB as one of the critical munitions it is looking to scale as quickly as possible.
Raytheon says the weapon can be fired from both ships and land to intercept short‑ to intermediate‑range ballistic missiles during the midcourse flight phase.

“SM-3 Block IB has proven its relevance in combat and this contract helps ensure we can replenish inventories and keep pace with the evolving threats the U.S. Navy, MDA [Missile Defense Agency] and their partners face around the world,” Raytheon President Phil Jasper said in a company release. (The MDA was the contracting agency for today’s deal.)
Back in February the DoD and Raytheon inked a framework agreement designed to pave the way for the multi-year deal.
Today’s announcement comes among a string of similar deals between the government and the RTX subsidiary.

In recent weeks, the duo inked a $24.4 billion deal designed to “accelerate” production of the Standard Missile-6, a $22.9 billion contract to ramp up production of the Tomahawk cruise missile to 1,000 rounds a year, and a deal worth up to nearly $20.7 billion for production of the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile (AMRAAM).

items.title: AWS launches open-source Physical AI Toolchain for robotics
items.originalTitle: AWS launches open-source Physical AI Toolchain for robotics
items.summary: Amazon Web Services (AWS) today launched an open-source Physical AI Toolchain designed to help roboticists move from collecting data to training, simulating, validating and deploying AI models on their robots. The toolchain brings together AWS services and NVIDIA’s Physical AI software stack into a single development workflow. The goal is to address one of the biggest challenges facing companies developing AI-powered robots: connecting the many pieces required to turn a trained model into a system that can reliably operate in the real world.

evidenceRecords.text: Amazon Web Services (AWS) today launched an open-source Physical AI Toolchain designed to help roboticists move from collecting data to training, simulating, validating and deploying AI models on their robots.
The toolchain brings together AWS services and NVIDIA’s Physical AI software stack into a single development workflow.

The goal is to address one of the biggest challenges facing companies developing AI-powered robots: connecting the many pieces required to turn a trained model into a system that can reliably operate in the real world.

“We’re trying to make this easy button, if you will, so that people can actually focus on the problem that they’re trying to solve rather than having to worry about all of the infrastructure,” Sri Elaprolu, director of Frontier AI Science and Engineering at AWS, told The Robot Report .
The Physical AI Toolchain is not a direct replacement for RoboMaker, a cloud-based robotics simulation platform that was shut down in 2025 .
Elaprolu described RoboMaker as one of the components of AWS’s robotics stack, while the new toolchain brings together a broader set of development technologies.

A robotics company could collect demonstrations of a robot performing a task, generate additional training scenarios synthetically, train or fine-tune a model, and test that model in simulation before deploying it to a physical robot.
Lessons from Amazon’s robots Elaprolu said the toolchain includes lessons from Amazon’s own robotics operations, which now include more than 1 million robots .
AWS is keeping the toolchain hardware-neutral.

“The toolchain is intentionally staying neutral to that final step.” Vulcan is Amazon’s first robot with a sense of touch, using sensors to pick and stow items at a fulfillment center. | Credit: Amazon Tactile sensing and construction Elaprolu also pointed to tactile sensing as an example of the specialized capabilities Physical AI may require.
An open-source approach The Physical AI Toolchain is open source, allowing startups and larger companies to use and modify it.
Elaprolu said the individual AWS and NVIDIA components have already been used by customers, including companies participating in AWS’s Physical AI Fellowship with MassRobotics and NVIDIA.

Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram.
It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East.

“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation.

Britain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine.
The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.
Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban.

Zafar Rustamkulov/NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer) space telescope is shedding light on brown dwarfs, celestial objects that blur the line between stars and exoplanets.
New findings published in The Astrophysical Journal show that these dark and cloudy worlds have chemically rich atmospheres not unlike the giant planets in our own solar system.
First discovered in the 1990s, brown dwarfs form from collapsing clouds of gas, like stars do, but they aren’t hefty enough to sustain hydrogen fusion in their cores.
Enter NASA’s SPHEREx , an infrared space telescope launched in March 2025 and managed by the agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

The study authors analyzed SPHEREx observations of 37 nearby brown dwarfs spanning the full brown dwarf temperature range, from about 4,000 to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit (2,200 to minus 20 degrees Celsius).

I really want to see what bounds the universe places on the variety of brown dwarfs.” “From orbit, SPHEREx sees wavelengths of light that are basically impossible to see with telescopes on the ground because water in Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them,” Rustamkulov said.
“We are picking up light from the deep, red clouds of brown dwarfs all over the sky.” Sweet spot Spotting brown dwarfs is something of a side project for SPHEREx.
For years, brown dwarfs have been spotted by other observatories, including NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope and retired Spitzer Space Telescope.
Thanks to its spectral coverage, NASA’s SPHEREx is revealing molecules like methane (CH4), carbon dioxide (CO2), and carbon monoxide (CO) in brown dwarf atmospheres.

items.title: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
items.originalTitle: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
items.summary: Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries. Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.

evidenceRecords.text: Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.

Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.

Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries.
Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.

Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea.
In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar.
Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city.

Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia.

Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.”
The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022.
Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died, according to British government estimates.
Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes.
Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize.

items.summary: The Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza. The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
The Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender.
She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice.
It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning.
She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues.
She responded in disbelief.

South Africa’s president Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

items.title: Anthropic's Claude Science creates the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky
items.originalTitle: Anthropic's Claude Science creates the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky
items.summary: Anthropic's Claude Science just mapped the entire sky in ultraviolet light for the first time. The project is supposed to show how AI can take over tedious data work that researchers would otherwise never get around to. Johns Hopkins astrophysicist Brice Ménard describes the process on the Anthropic website. UV light reveals dust lit up by starlight, things like clouds around young stars or rings left behind by stellar explosions. A complete UV map didn't exist until now because the ozone layer blocks UV light, so it can only be measured from space.

evidenceRecords.text: Astrophysicist Brice Ménard of Johns Hopkins University used Anthropic's Claude Science to map the entire sky in ultraviolet light for the first time.
The article Anthropic's Claude Science creates the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky appeared first on The Decoder .
Anthropic's Claude Science just mapped the entire sky in ultraviolet light for the first time.
The project is supposed to show how AI can take over tedious data work that researchers would otherwise never get around to.
Johns Hopkins astrophysicist Brice Ménard describes the process on the Anthropic website.
UV light reveals dust lit up by starlight, things like clouds around young stars or rings left behind by stellar explosions.
A complete UV map didn't exist until now because the ozone layer blocks UV light, so it can only be measured from space.
NASA's GALEX mission covered about two-thirds of the sky but skipped bright star-forming regions.
Claude Science coordinates AI agents that downloaded data from multiple space missions, calibrated it, and merged it together.
They filled missing areas using inpainting, a technique where a model learns from existing data to reconstruct gaps.
In tests, predictions averaged about ten percent deviation from actual measurements.
The map is meant to serve as teaching material.
Ménard suspects many scientists have been putting off similar projects that AI could now make possible.
Source: Anthropic / UV Sky Map

items.title: Fired researchers accuse OpenAI of 'chilling' safety efforts
items.originalTitle: Fired researchers accuse OpenAI of 'chilling' safety efforts
items.summary: Three former OpenAI security researchers on Thursday accused the ChatGPT maker of firing them for warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence, reigniting the debate over safety at a company whose software has been involved in security breaches. "I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," one of the fired staffers, Mikita Balesni, wrote on X, breaking a weeklong silence since their very public dismissal. Balesni and the two other fired employees, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, publicly shared a letter to OpenAI on Thursday.

Homes that are nearly a century old are getting a new life at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, preserving their historic character while providing updated features and addressing safety concerns.
They were built between 1928 and 1939, and feature elements including stucco walls, copper gutters, hardwood floors and basements.
But these aren’t even the oldest of Army housing.
There are 867 houses built before 1919, located on 19 other Army installations in 13 states and the District of Columbia, according to the Army.
At Fort Bragg, about 2,300 of the base’s 6,104 homes were built before 1960, officials said.
The Army manages the largest inventory of historic housing in the federal government, with more than 30,000 historic homes that are more than 50 years old.
These homes are subject to the requirements of the National Historic Preservation Act, according to the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation.

That federal agency’s mission is to promote the preservation of America’s historic places and has worked with the Army and the other services as they prepare plans to renovate these houses, making sure they preserve the historic character while meeting the needs of families.

“These residences are an important part of Fort Bragg’s history, but their greatest value is continuing to serve soldiers and families who live in these homes,” said Col. Luke Wittmer, the installation’s garrison commander, in an announcement. “This renovation preserves history while ensuring we continue to meet the needs of today’s families.”
Historic homes have long been a challenge to preserve and maintain for military families, with a variety of issues such as lead paint and asbestos, which are both hazardous and costly to remediate.

items.originalTitle: Zankore's AI factory: Can Central Java afford the water cost?
items.summary: The 1-gigawatt (GW) AI Factory will be built in stages. evidenceRecords.text: The 1-gigawatt (GW) AI Factory will be built in stages.
Its first phase, with a capacity of about 200 megawatts (MW), is scheduled to begin construction in Batang, Central Java, in the first half of 2027.
The project is being promoted as a step toward Indonesia's ambition to become a regional AI hub.
But advanced AI infrastructure requires not only enormous amounts of electricity.
Its servers also need large volumes of water for cooling.
The difficult question is whether the government can guarantee enough water for both AI servers and local communities when Central Java is already facing water stress.
Every time we ask a chatbot a question, thousands of chips in data centers process the request and generate heat.
Cooling systems must continuously remove that heat, often by evaporating water through cooling towers.
Water is also consumed indirectly along the data center supply chain, including in electricity generation.
A 2025 study by University of California researchers estimated potential water demand from AI factories using Microsoft's projected approach.
Indonesia recorded the highest projected cooling-water consumption among the countries examined, at about 1.9 liters for every kilowatt-hour of electricity used by servers.

Based on those projections, Zankore's 200-MW first phase could evaporate between 4.8 million and 9.1 million liters (1.3 million and 2.4 million gallons) of water per day, assuming continuous operation.

At that rate, Zankore could consume an amount equivalent to the 75.46 million liters (19.9 million gallons) of clean water prepared by the Central Java government during the 2026 drought crisis in just eight to 16 days.
